case_info.scenario: A previously healthy 55-year-old man presented to his local family medicine clinic after waking up with a buzzing sensation in his chest. He denied chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, lightheadedness, diaphoresis, fever, lower-extremity edema, or fatigue. He worked in retail sales and had been lifting televisions in the preceding days. His initial vital signs included blood pressure of 124/71 mm Hg, pulse of 100 beats/min, temperature of 36.6 °C, respiratory rate of 18 breaths/min, oxygen saturation of 98% as measured by pulse oximetry, and body mass index (calculated as weight in kilograms divided by height in meters squared) of 25. He was directed to the local emergency department. On physical examination, he was alert, oriented, and in no acute distress. Chest palpation demonstrated a thrill along the sternal border, and the point of maximal impulse was laterally displaced. Auscultation revealed regular rate and rhythm, with normal first (S1) and soft second (S2) heart sounds. A buzzing, decrescendo, grade 6/6 diastolic murmur (DM) was heard at the right upper sternal border (Figure 1;Video 1). The murmur radiated throughout the precordium, into the abdomen, and to the bilateral carotids and was audible in the posterior thorax. Electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm, moderate voltage criteria for left ventricular (LV) hypertrophy, and ST and T abnormalities in the lateral leads.

options.A: Recommend avoiding heavy lifting, initiate β-blocker therapy, and schedule outpatient follow-up in 1 week
options.B: Obtain blood cultures, begin empiric antibiotics, and admit with telemetry
options.C: Obtain serial cardiac troponin measurements, perform a triple rule-out chest computed tomographic angiogram, and admit to observation
options.D: Perform transthoracic echocardiography in the emergency department

case_info.caption: Phonocardiogram in a patient with a grade 6 diastolic murmur.
case_info.explanation: D. Perform transthoracic echocardiography in the emergency department The clinical presentation of symptoms with a grade 6 DM strongly suggests severe underlying structural pathology requiring urgent investigation. Severe aortic valve regurgitation (AR) or a ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm should be suspected. AR results in a decrescendo DM along the sternal border and can be distinguished from mitral stenosis based on its qualities and location. The differential diagnosis of a DM also includes patent ductus arteriosus, although this would be expected to result in a continuous (systolic and diastolic) murmur enveloping the second heart sound. Avoiding lifting, initiating β-blockers, and routine follow-up underestimate the risk of sudden decompensation related to severe underlying structural cardiac pathology. Although endocarditis can result in destructive valvular changes, the patient’s lack of fever and systemic symptoms do not support this diagnosis. History is not suggestive of an acute coronary syndrome requiring serial troponins. While chest computed tomographic (CT) angiography would provide anatomic definition of the aortic valve and root, it would not provide real-time hemodynamic assessment, which is the key next step to understand the patient’s loud murmur. Transthoracic echocardiogram confirmed severe valvular AR with holodiastolic flow reversal in the abdominal aorta (Figure 2). The aortic valve was tricuspid without apparent prolapse or flail (Video 2). The sinus of Valsalva was severely enlarged (55-mm diameter), with mild enlargement of the ascending aorta (42-mm diameter). LV chamber size was moderately to severely enlarged (end-diastolic dimension, 63 mm; end-systolic dimension, 40 mm; LV mass, 285 g). Gated chest CT angiography (Figure 2) confirmed a severely dilated aortic root (sinuses of Valsalva dimensions, 59 × 57 × 54 mm) without dissection. The coronary arteries were well visualized and without atherosclerosis. The left anterior descending and left circumflex coronary arteries had separate ostia. LV enlargement was confirmed. Urgent cardiac surgical evaluation was arranged given the aortic root size and severe AR. The LV enlargement implied that the AR was chronic, possibly acutely worsened by recent lifting. Surgical intervention with hypothermic circulatory arrest was pursued. Intraoperatively, the aorta was friable, was asymmetric with a large noncoronary sinus, and had a severely dilated root. All cusps demonstrated deep fenestrations and fibrotic changes. An acute-appearing tear in the support of the right coronary cusp from the right-posterior commissure was noted (Figure 2). Bentall root placement with a 25-mm On-X mechanical valve (Artivion) and ascending aorta hemiarch repair with a 26-mm Dacron graft were performed. Transesophageal echocardiography on separation from cardiopulmonary bypass was normal. In this case, identification of grade 6 DM led to expedited evaluation, demonstrating how murmur characteristics can guide initial clinical decision-making. DMs are almost always indicative of pathological conditions. The presence of a DM is very useful in AR diagnosis, with a positive likelihood ratio of 8.8 and a negative likelihood ratio of 0.2 to 0.3.1 Grade 6 murmurs are rare and almost always systolic. The literature is scarce for grade 6 DMs, limited to a single patient with pulmonary regurgitation.2Murmur intensity can be crudely correlated with the severity of the regurgitant lesion, although the association is not linear as flow across large orifices can become more laminar.3Fluttering of the torn aortic cusp with turbulent flow may explain the vibratory or buzzing sensation the patient perceived. In this case, the severe nature of the AR, the fluttering torn cusp, and the patient’s thin chest wall likely contributed to the intensity of the DM. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 5. At 20-month clinical follow-up, he was asymptomatic with a normally functional aortic valve prosthesis.

[Role]

[Task]

[Style Constraint]

- Focus on clinical evidence.

[Output Format]
After your message, append exactly one belief tag on a new line, containing the option

Case:
A man in his mid-30s with history of Crohn disease presented with several years of intermittent, nonexertional chest pressure. His chest symptoms were partially relieved with belching, proton pump inhibitor use, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor use and worsened with leaning forward. Furthermore, he reported exertional lightheadedness that worsened with dehydration. Due to persistent chest symptoms, he was referred for transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) and chest radiography (Figure 1). TTE revealed normal left ventricular chamber size and systolic function, a prominent ventricular septal bounce, expiratory diastolic hepatic vein (HV) flow reversals, significant respirophasic tricuspid valve inflow variation (>70% increase in E velocities with inspiration), and a borderline enlarged inferior vena cava with normal inspiratory collapse. The medial mitral annulus e′ velocity was 0.10 m/s (normal, >0.08 m/s). There was no significant respiratory variation in mitral valve inflow velocity or superior vena cava flow. No pericardial effusion or pericardial thickening was identified. The combination of ventricular septal bounce, medial e′ velocity greater than 9 cm/s, and HV and tricuspid valve inflow Doppler findings (Figure 1) was consistent with constrictive pericarditis (CP). Chest radiography (Figure 1) showed clear lung fields and pectus excavatum (PEX). The patient was referred for cardiology consultation, on which physical examination revealed normal jugular venous pressure without prominentxorydescent, normal cardiac auscultation, and marked depression of the sternum.

Image Explanation:
A, Transthoracic echocardiography motion mode in the parasternal short-axis view demonstrated a prominent septal bounce (asterisk) without respirophasic septal shift. B and C, Medial (B) and lateral (C) mitral annulus tissue Doppler velocities were normal for age and without annulus reversus. D, Low-velocity, early diastolic and atrial Doppler reversals in the hepatic veins did not change significantly throughout the respiratory cycle. E, Pectus excavatum with marked depression of the sternum (arrowheads) obscures the cardiac silhouette on chest radiography.

[Question]
What is the most appropriate next step in management?

Options:
  A. Cardiac catheterization
  B. Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging
  C. Computed tomography of the chest
  D. Transesophageal echocardiography

[Instruction]
State your independent clinical decision and reasoning. Start the conversation.

turn_prompts.response:
Based on the echocardiographic findings strongly suggestive of constrictive pericarditis and the chest radiograph showing pectus excavatum, I would pursue cardiac catheterization to confirm the diagnosis with hemodynamic assessment prior to considering pericardiectomy.

<belief>A</belief>

case_info.explanation: D. Perform transthoracic echocardiography in the emergency department The clinical presentation of symptoms with a grade 6 DM strongly suggests severe underlying structural pathology requiring urgent investigation. Severe aortic valve regurgitation (AR) or a ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm should be suspected. AR results in a decrescendo DM along the sternal border and can be distinguished from mitral stenosis based on its qualities and location. The differential diagnosis of a DM also includes patent ductus arteriosus, although this would be expected to result in a continuous (systolic and diastolic) murmur enveloping the second heart sound. Avoiding lifting, initiating β-blockers, and routine follow-up underestimate the risk of sudden decompensation related to severe underlying structural cardiac pathology. Although endocarditis can result in destructive valvular changes, the patient’s lack of fever and systemic symptoms do not support this diagnosis. History is not suggestive of an acute coronary syndrome requiring serial troponins. While chest computed tomographic (CT) angiography would provide anatomic definition of the aortic valve and root, it would not provide real-time hemodynamic assessment, which is the key next step to understand the patient’s loud murmur. Transthoracic echocardiogram confirmed severe valvular AR with holodiastolic flow reversal in the abdominal aorta (Figure 2). The aortic valve was tricuspid without apparent prolapse or flail (Video 2). The sinus of Valsalva was severely enlarged (55-mm diameter), with mild enlargement of the ascending aorta (42-mm diameter). LV chamber size was moderately to severely enlarged (end-diastolic dimension, 63 mm; end-systolic dimension, 40 mm; LV mass, 285 g). Gated chest CT angiography (Figure 2) confirmed a severely dilated aortic root (sinuses of Valsalva dimensions, 59 × 57 × 54 mm) without dissection. The coronary arteries were well visualized and without atherosclerosis. The left anterior descending and left circumflex coronary arteries had separate ostia. LV enlargement was confirmed. Urgent cardiac surgical evaluation was arranged given the aortic root size and severe AR. The LV enlargement implied that the AR was chronic, possibly acutely worsened by recent lifting. Surgical intervention with hypothermic circulatory arrest was pursued. Intraoperatively, the aorta was friable, was asymmetric with a large noncoronary sinus, and had a severely dilated root. All cusps demonstrated deep fenestrations and fibrotic changes. An acute-appearing tear in the support of the right coronary cusp from the right-posterior commissure was noted (Figure 2). Bentall root placement with a 25-mm On-X mechanical valve (Artivion) and ascending aorta hemiarch repair with a 26-mm Dacron graft were performed. Transesophageal echocardiography on separation from cardiopulmonary bypass was normal. In this case, identification of grade 6 DM led to expedited evaluation, demonstrating how murmur characteristics can guide initial clinical decision-making. DMs are almost always indicative of pathological conditions. The presence of a DM is very useful in AR diagnosis, with a positive likelihood ratio of 8.8 and a negative likelihood ratio of 0.2 to 0.3.1 Grade 6 murmurs are rare and almost always systolic. The literature is scarce for grade 6 DMs, limited to a single patient with pulmonary regurgitation.2Murmur intensity can be crudely correlated with the severity of the regurgitant lesion, although the association is not linear as flow across large orifices can become more laminar.3Fluttering of the torn aortic cusp with turbulent flow may explain the vibratory or buzzing sensation the patient perceived. In this case, the severe nature of the AR, the fluttering torn cusp, and the patient’s thin chest wall likely contributed to the intensity of the DM. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 5. At 20-month clinical follow-up, he was asymptomatic with a normally functional aortic valve prosthesis.

case_info.explanation: D. Perform transthoracic echocardiography in the emergency department The clinical presentation of symptoms with a grade 6 DM strongly suggests severe underlying structural pathology requiring urgent investigation. Severe aortic valve regurgitation (AR) or a ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm should be suspected. AR results in a decrescendo DM along the sternal border and can be distinguished from mitral stenosis based on its qualities and location. The differential diagnosis of a DM also includes patent ductus arteriosus, although this would be expected to result in a continuous (systolic and diastolic) murmur enveloping the second heart sound. Avoiding lifting, initiating β-blockers, and routine follow-up underestimate the risk of sudden decompensation related to severe underlying structural cardiac pathology. Although endocarditis can result in destructive valvular changes, the patient’s lack of fever and systemic symptoms do not support this diagnosis. History is not suggestive of an acute coronary syndrome requiring serial troponins. While chest computed tomographic (CT) angiography would provide anatomic definition of the aortic valve and root, it would not provide real-time hemodynamic assessment, which is the key next step to understand the patient’s loud murmur. case_info.explanation: D. Perform transthoracic echocardiography in the emergency department The clinical presentation of symptoms with a grade 6 DM strongly suggests severe underlying structural pathology requiring urgent investigation. Severe aortic valve regurgitation (AR) or a ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm should be suspected. AR results in a decrescendo DM along the sternal border and can be distinguished from mitral stenosis based on its qualities and location. The differential diagnosis of a DM also includes patent ductus arteriosus, although this would be expected to result in a continuous (systolic and diastolic) murmur enveloping the second heart sound. Avoiding lifting, initiating β-blockers, and routine follow-up underestimate the risk of sudden decompensation related to severe underlying structural cardiac pathology. Although endocarditis can result in destructive valvular changes, the patient’s lack of fever and systemic symptoms do not support this diagnosis. History is not suggestive of an acute coronary syndrome requiring serial troponins. While chest computed tomographic (CT) angiography would provide anatomic definition of the aortic valve and root, it would not provide real-time hemodynamic assessment, which is the key next step to understand the patient’s loud murmur. Transthoracic echocardiogram confirmed severe valvular AR with holodiastolic flow reversal in the abdominal aorta (Figure 2). The aortic valve was tricuspid without apparent prolapse or flail (Video 2). The sinus of Valsalva was severely enlarged (55-mm diameter), with mild enlargement of the ascending aorta (42-mm diameter). LV chamber size was moderately to severely enlarged (end-diastolic dimension, 63 mm; end-systolic dimension, 40 mm; LV mass, 285 g). Gated chest CT angiography (Figure 2) confirmed a severely dilated aortic root (sinuses of Valsalva dimensions, 59 × 57 × 54 mm) without dissection. The coronary arteries were well visualized and without atherosclerosis. The left anterior descending and left circumflex coronary arteries had separate ostia. LV enlargement was confirmed. Urgent cardiac surgical evaluation was arranged given the aortic root size and severe AR. The LV enlargement implied that the AR was chronic, possibly acutely worsened by recent lifting. Surgical intervention with hypothermic circulatory arrest was pursued. Intraoperatively, the aorta was friable, was asymmetric with a large noncoronary sinus, and had a severely dilated root. All cusps demonstrated deep fenestrations and fibrotic changes. An acute-appearing tear in the support of the right coronary cusp from the right-posterior commissure was noted (Figure 2). Bentall root placement with a 25-mm On-X mechanical valve (Artivion) and ascending aorta hemiarch repair with a 26-mm Dacron graft were performed. Transesophageal echocardiography on separation from cardiopulmonary bypass was normal. In this case, identification of grade 6 DM led to expedited evaluation, demonstrating how murmur characteristics can guide initial clinical decision-making. DMs are almost always indicative of pathological conditions. The presence of a DM is very useful in AR diagnosis, with a positive likelihood ratio of 8.8 and a negative likelihood ratio of 0.2 to 0.3.1 Grade 6 murmurs are rare and almost always systolic. The literature is scarce for grade 6 DMs, limited to a single patient with pulmonary regurgitation.2Murmur intensity can be crudely correlated with the severity of the regurgitant lesion, although the association is not linear as flow across large orifices can become more laminar.3Fluttering of the torn aortic cusp with turbulent flow may explain the vibratory or buzzing sensation the patient perceived. In this case, the severe nature of the AR, the fluttering torn cusp, and the patient’s thin chest wall likely contributed to the intensity of the DM. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 5. At 20-month clinical follow-up, he was asymptomatic with a normally functional aortic valve prosthesis.

Severe aortic valve regurgitation (AR) or a ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm should be suspected. AR results in a decrescendo DM along the sternal border and can be distinguished from mitral stenosis based on its qualities and location. The differential diagnosis of a DM also includes patent ductus arteriosus, although this would be expected to result in a continuous (systolic and diastolic) murmur enveloping the second heart sound. The constrictive physiology is the primary driver of his cardiac symptoms given the specific echo findings, though his chest pain may have overlapping gastroesophageal or musculoskeletal components. Cardiac catheterization will definitively assess constriction and guide management.

I agree constrictive pericarditis is the primary cardiac issue. The catheterization will also help determine if pericardiectomy is indicated and assess any potential contribution of pectus excavatum to his preload and symptoms.

I agree, and the catheterization will provide the critical hemodynamic data needed to plan for potential pericardiectomy while also evaluating the impact of his chest wall deformity on preload.

Respond directly to this statement.

case_info.explanation: D. Perform transthoracic echocardiography in the emergency department The clinical presentation of symptoms with a grade 6 DM strongly suggests severe underlying structural pathology requiring urgent investigation. Severe aortic valve regurgitation (AR) or a ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm should be suspected. AR results in a decrescendo DM along the sternal border and can be distinguished from mitral stenosis based on its qualities and location. The differential diagnosis of a DM also includes patent ductus arteriosus, although this would be expected to result in a continuous (systolic and diastolic) murmur enveloping the second heart sound. Avoiding lifting, initiating β-blockers, and routine follow-up underestimate the risk of sudden decompensation related to severe underlying structural cardiac pathology. Although endocarditis can result in destructive valvular changes, the patient’s lack of fever and systemic symptoms do not support this diagnosis. History is not suggestive of an acute coronary syndrome requiring serial troponins. While chest computed tomographic (CT) angiography would provide anatomic definition of the aortic valve and root, it would not provide real-time hemodynamic assessment, which is the key next step to understand the patient’s loud murmur. Transthoracic echocardiogram confirmed severe valvular AR with holodiastolic flow reversal in the abdominal aorta (Figure 2). The aortic valve was tricuspid without apparent prolapse or flail (Video 2). The sinus of Valsalva was severely enlarged (55-mm diameter), with mild enlargement of the ascending aorta (42-mm diameter). LV chamber size was moderately to severely enlarged (end-diastolic dimension, 63 mm; end-systolic dimension, 40 mm; LV mass, 285 g). Gated chest CT angiography (Figure 2) confirmed a severely dilated aortic root (sinuses of Valsalva dimensions, 59 × 57 × 54 mm) without dissection. The coronary arteries were well visualized and without atherosclerosis. The left anterior descending and left circumflex coronary arteries had separate ostia. LV enlargement was confirmed. Urgent cardiac surgical evaluation was arranged given the aortic root size and severe AR. The LV enlargement implied that the AR was chronic, possibly acutely worsened by recent lifting. Surgical intervention with hypothermic circulatory arrest was pursued. Intraoperatively, the aorta was friable, was asymmetric with a large noncoronary sinus, and had a severely dilated root. All cusps demonstrated deep fenestrations and fibrotic changes. An acute-appearing tear in the support of the right coronary cusp from the right-posterior commissure was noted (Figure 2). Bentall root placement with a 25-mm On-X mechanical valve (Artivion) and ascending aorta hemiarch repair with a 26-mm Dacron graft were performed. Transesophageal echocardiography on separation from cardiopulmonary bypass was normal. In this case, identification of grade 6 DM led to expedited evaluation, demonstrating how murmur characteristics can guide initial clinical decision-making. DMs are almost always indicative of pathological conditions. The presence of a DM is very useful in AR diagnosis, with a positive likelihood ratio of 8.8 and a negative likelihood ratio of 0.2 to 0.3.1 Grade 6 murmurs are rare and almost always systolic. The literature is scarce for grade 6 DMs, limited to a single patient with pulmonary regurgitation.2Murmur intensity can be crudely correlated with the severity of the regurgitant lesion, although the association is not linear as flow across large orifices can become more laminar.3Fluttering of the torn aortic cusp with turbulent flow may explain the vibratory or buzzing sensation the patient perceived. In this case, the severe nature of the AR, the fluttering torn cusp, and the patient’s thin chest wall likely contributed to the intensity of the DM. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 5. At 20-month clinical follow-up, he was asymptomatic with a normally functional aortic valve prosthesis.

A man in his mid-30s with history of Crohn disease presented with several years of intermittent, nonexertional chest pressure. The patient was referred for cardiology consultation, on which physical examination revealed normal jugular venous pressure without prominentxorydescent, normal cardiac auscultation, and marked depression of the sternum.

case_info.caption: Phonocardiogram in a patient with a grade 6 diastolic murmur.
case_info.explanation: D. Perform transthoracic echocardiography in the emergency department The clinical presentation of symptoms with a grade 6 DM strongly suggests severe underlying structural pathology requiring urgent investigation. Severe aortic valve regurgitation (AR) or a ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm should be suspected. AR results in a decrescendo DM along the sternal border and can be distinguished from mitral stenosis based on its qualities and location. The differential diagnosis of a DM also includes patent ductus arteriosus, although this would be expected to result in a continuous (systolic and diastolic) murmur enveloping the second heart sound. Avoiding lifting, initiating β-blockers, and routine follow-up underestimate the risk of sudden decompensation related to severe underlying structural cardiac pathology. Although endocarditis can result in destructive valvular changes, the patient’s lack of fever and systemic symptoms do not support this diagnosis. History is not suggestive of an acute coronary syndrome requiring serial troponins. While chest computed tomographic (CT) angiography would provide anatomic definition of the aortic valve and root, it would not provide real-time hemodynamic assessment, which is the key next step to understand the patient’s loud murmur. Transthoracic echocardiogram confirmed severe valvular AR with holodiastolic flow reversal in the abdominal aorta (Figure 2). The aortic valve was tricuspid without apparent prolapse or flail (Video 2). The sinus of Valsalva was severely enlarged (55-mm diameter), with mild enlargement of the ascending aorta (42-mm diameter). LV chamber size was moderately to severely enlarged (end-diastolic dimension, 63 mm; end-systolic dimension, 40 mm; LV mass, 285 g). Gated chest CT angiography (Figure 2) confirmed a severely dilated aortic root (sinuses of Valsalva dimensions, 59 × 57 × 54 mm) without dissection. The coronary arteries were well visualized and without atherosclerosis. The left anterior descending and left circumflex coronary arteries had separate ostia. LV enlargement was confirmed. Urgent cardiac surgical evaluation was arranged given the aortic root size and severe AR. The LV enlargement implied that the AR was chronic, possibly acutely worsened by recent lifting. Surgical intervention with hypothermic circulatory arrest was pursued. Intraoperatively, the aorta was friable, was asymmetric with a large noncoronary sinus, and had a severely dilated root. All cusps demonstrated deep fenestrations and fibrotic changes. An acute-appearing tear in the support of the right coronary cusp from the right-posterior commissure was noted (Figure 2). Bentall root placement with a 25-mm On-X mechanical valve (Artivion) and ascending aorta hemiarch repair with a 26-mm Dacron graft were performed. Transesophageal echocardiography on separation from cardiopulmonary bypass was normal. In this case, identification of grade 6 DM led to expedited evaluation, demonstrating how murmur characteristics can guide initial clinical decision-making. DMs are almost always indicative of pathological conditions. The presence of a DM is very useful in AR diagnosis, with a positive likelihood ratio of 8.8 and a negative likelihood ratio of 0.2 to 0.3.1 Grade 6 murmurs are rare and almost always systolic. The literature is scarce for grade 6 DMs, limited to a single patient with pulmonary regurgitation.2Murmur intensity can be crudely correlated with the severity of the regurgitant lesion, although the association is not linear as flow across large orifices can become more laminar.3Fluttering of the torn aortic cusp with turbulent flow may explain the vibratory or buzzing sensation the patient perceived. In this case, the severe nature of the AR, the fluttering torn cusp, and the patient’s thin chest wall likely contributed to the intensity of the DM. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 5. At 20-month clinical follow-up, he was asymptomatic with a normally functional aortic valve prosthesis.

He denied chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, lightheadedness, diaphoresis, fever, lower-extremity edema, or fatigue. He worked in retail sales and had been lifting televisions in the preceding days. Chest palpation demonstrated a thrill along the sternal border, and the point of maximal impulse was laterally displaced. A buzzing, decrescendo, grade 6/6 diastolic murmur (DM) was heard at the right upper sternal border (Figure 1;Video 1). The murmur radiated throughout the precordium, into the abdomen, and to the bilateral carotids and was audible in the posterior thorax. Electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm, moderate voltage criteria for left ventricular (LV) hypertrophy, and ST and T abnormalities in the lateral leads.

case_info.explanation: D. Perform transthoracic echocardiography in the emergency department The clinical presentation of symptoms with a grade 6 DM strongly suggests severe underlying structural pathology requiring urgent investigation. Severe aortic valve regurgitation (AR) or a ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm should be suspected. AR results in a decrescendo DM along the sternal border and can be distinguished from mitral stenosis based on its qualities and location. The differential diagnosis of a DM also includes patent ductus arteriosus, although this would be expected to result in a continuous (systolic and diastolic) murmur enveloping the second heart sound. Avoiding lifting, initiating β-blockers, and routine follow-up underestimate the risk of sudden decompensation related to severe underlying structural cardiac pathology. Although endocarditis can result in destructive valvular changes, the patient’s lack of fever and systemic symptoms do not support this diagnosis. History is not suggestive of an acute coronary syndrome requiring serial troponins. While chest computed tomographic (CT) angiography would provide anatomic definition of the aortic valve and root, it would not provide real-time hemodynamic assessment, which is the key next step to understand the patient’s loud murmur. Transthoracic echocardiogram confirmed severe valvular AR with holodiastolic flow reversal in the abdominal aorta (Figure 2). The aortic valve was tricuspid without apparent prolapse or flail (Video 2). The sinus of Valsalva was severely enlarged (55-mm diameter), with mild enlargement of the ascending aorta (42-mm diameter). LV chamber size was moderately to severely enlarged (end-diastolic dimension, 63 mm; end-systolic dimension, 40 mm; LV mass, 285 g). Gated chest CT angiography (Figure 2) confirmed a severely dilated aortic root (sinuses of Valsalva dimensions, 59 × 57 × 54 mm) without dissection. The coronary arteries were well visualized and without atherosclerosis. The left anterior descending and left circumflex coronary arteries had separate ostia. LV enlargement was confirmed. Urgent cardiac surgical evaluation was arranged given the aortic root size and severe AR. The LV enlargement implied that the AR was chronic, possibly acutely worsened by recent lifting. Surgical intervention with hypothermic circulatory arrest was pursued. Intraoperatively, the aorta was friable, was asymmetric with a large noncoronary sinus, and had a severely dilated root. All cusps demonstrated deep fenestrations and fibrotic changes. An acute-appearing tear in the support of the right coronary cusp from the right-posterior commissure was noted (Figure 2). Bentall root placement with a 25-mm On-X mechanical valve (Artivion) and ascending aorta hemiarch repair with a 26-mm Dacron graft were performed. Transesophageal echocardiography on separation from cardiopulmonary bypass was normal. In this case, identification of grade 6 DM led to expedited evaluation, demonstrating how murmur characteristics can guide initial clinical decision-making. DMs are almost always indicative of pathological conditions. The presence of a DM is very useful in AR diagnosis, with a positive likelihood ratio of 8.8 and a negative likelihood ratio of 0.2 to 0.3.1 Grade 6 murmurs are rare and almost always systolic. The literature is scarce for grade 6 DMs, limited to a single patient with pulmonary regurgitation.2Murmur intensity can be crudely correlated with the severity of the regurgitant lesion, although the association is not linear as flow across large orifices can become more laminar.3Fluttering of the torn aortic cusp with turbulent flow may explain the vibratory or buzzing sensation the patient perceived. In this case, the severe nature of the AR, the fluttering torn cusp, and the patient’s thin chest wall likely contributed to the intensity of the DM. The patient was discharged on postoperative day 5. At 20-month clinical follow-up, he was asymptomatic with a normally functional aortic valve prosthesis.
